The tramway that outlived its river

By Probe Fixtures · 9 min read

When the last barge left the lower quay in the autumn of 1931, the town's council assumed the tramway that had carried its coal and its passengers along the embankment would follow within the year. The river had been the reason for the line: a narrow-gauge spur from the mill to the wharf, laid by a company that expected the water traffic to double and instead watched it halve. Yet the tramway ran for another sixty years, and the story of how it did so is a story about habits, about who owns a right of way once the reason for it has gone, and about the odd durability of small public things.

The line was never fast. Its cars, bought second-hand from a coastal resort that had electrified early and regretted it, managed twelve miles an hour on the flat and rather less on the climb past the gasworks. Schoolchildren timed their walks against it and usually won. But it stopped where people lived, at the ends of streets rather than the middle of a bypass, and it stopped often; a woman with a pram could board it without help, which was more than the buses that replaced the river ferries could say for themselves.

Ownership passed, over the decades, from the mill company to a trust, from the trust to the borough, and from the borough to a preservation society whose members were mostly the drivers who had refused to retire. Each transfer was contested, and each contest was settled by the same discovery: that the deeds granted the tramway its strip of embankment in perpetuity, and that removing the rails would cost more than running the cars. Inertia, it turned out, could be a civic policy as well as a private failing.

What the embankment kept

Walk the route today and the river is a culvert under a supermarket car park, but the embankment is intact. It kept the tramway; the tramway, in turn, kept a line of trees that the company had planted for shade, a row of shelters with cast-iron brackets that a foundry no longer in business had signed in raised letters, and a pattern of small shops that faced the stops rather than the road. Planners who later studied the district found its footfall stubbornly higher than the model predicted and could not, for some years, say why.

There is a temptation to make the story a parable, and the town's tourist office has largely given in to it. The truth is more particular. The line survived because it was cheap to run, because the people who ran it were paid little and asked for less, because the rails were laid on a route nobody else wanted, and because a handful of clerks in three successive offices read the deeds carefully before signing anything. None of those conditions was designed, and none of them would be easy to reproduce on purpose.

The cars still run on summer weekends. They are slower now, with a speed limit imposed after an inspector noticed the age of the brakes, and the drivers are younger than the society's founders ever expected to recruit. The river is not coming back. The tramway, against every forecast made about it, has not gone anywhere.
